key_concept: Phyllotaxy (Greek phyllon = leaf, taxis = arrangement) is the pattern in which leaves are arranged on the stem or branch.
steps: Break the word down: 'phyllo' means leaf and 'taxy' means arrangement, so phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves.
Phyllotaxy has three main types. In alternate phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node (e.g., China rose, mustard, sunflower).
In opposite phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arises at each node, opposite each other (e.g., Calotropis, guava).
In whorled phyllotaxy, more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl (e.g., Alstonia).
The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is a different term, called inflorescence. So the correct answer is leaves.
why_not_others: The arrangement of flowers is called inflorescence. Sepals belong to the calyx, and the arrangement of sepals or petals within a floral whorl is called aestivation. Fruits have no special arrangement term of this kind.
common_trap: Students mix up phyllotaxy (leaves on the stem), aestivation (sepals or petals in a bud) and inflorescence (flowers on an axis).
time_saving_tip: Remember the root 'phyll-' (as in chlorophyll and phylloclade), which always refers to the leaf. That lets you answer instantly.
